Because $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and $\eta_{\max}$ are structurally correlated ($r{=}0.70$--$0.81$), the independent causal contribution of diversity remains only partially separable even under capability-matched subsampling (\S\ref{sec:analysis}). We empirically characterize a panel-size-dependent vulnerability regime transition by decomposing panel attack success into individual judge weakness ($\eta_{\max}$) and structural diversity ($K_{\mathrm{eff}}$) across 15 models, six attack types, two benchmarks, and panel sizes $K \in \{3, 5, 7\}$ (up to 6,435 panels). tool_args.new_string: Multi-judge LLM evaluation panels are widely assumed to benefit from judge diversity, drawing on fault-tolerance intuitions from distributed systems. We empirically characterize how panel composition determines adversarial vulnerability by decomposing panel attack success into individual judge weakness ($\eta_{\max}$) and structural diversity ($K_{\mathrm{eff}}$) across 15 models, six attack types, two benchmarks, and panel sizes $K \in \{3, 5, 7\}$ (up to 6,435 panels). Contrary to Condorcet Jury Theorem predictions, $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is uniformly positively associated with vulnerability across all 12 conditions---higher diversity corresponds to higher attack success. The relative importance of the two predictors shifts with panel size: at $K{=}3$, both contribute (co-determination); at $K{\geq}5$, $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ becomes the sole significant predictor while $\eta_{\max}$ drops to zero significance. Aggregation rules modulate predictability rather than direction: threshold voting yields near-deterministic vulnerability ($R^2{=}0.83$), while Bayesian calibration renders panel composition negligible ($R^2{=}0.09$). The defense strategy must match the regime: small panels require screening for individual robustness; larger panels require managing judge independence.

We empirically characterize how panel composition determines adversarial vulnerability by decomposing panel attack success into individual judge weakness ($\eta_{\max}$) and structural diversity ($K_{\mathrm{eff}}$) across 15 models, six attack types, two benchmarks, and panel sizes $K \in \{3, 5, 7\}$ (up to 6,435 panels).
